findings.element: The owner's status line .b-shared and the primary verb, after Copy the link on state=publish
findings.problem: Driven at 1440x960 with clipboard permission granted, from state=owner-draft: press Publish, press Copy the link (the live token is verifiably on the clipboard — readText returns https://timeline.signalstudio.ie/s/j7Qm2...), press Back to the plan. The plan then says "Only you can see this" and the primary control still says "Publish". The owner has just put a working link into a message and the surface asserts nobody can see it, while offering to do a thing already done. The code states the intended model verbatim at render-b.js:1268 — "Taking the link IS the publish in this model, so the verb, the status line and the press heading flip once, together, at the moment it becomes someone else's" — but that branch lives in wireOwner's data-act="copy" handler, and the owner surface has no copy control (its bar is Add a moment / Preview / Get the link), so it is unreachable. states.publish has its own copy handler, which writes "Copied" and "Link copied." and never touches F.publication; the press headline stays "Send it to Mara & Finn." on a second visit too. This is the class the file already records as fixed once at render-b.js:1467 ("the primary control said 'Publish' — offering to do a thing that had already been done"), returned on the draft branch round 9 built. It restates no gate: interaction-check.mjs:2933 is headed "draft commits; taking the link publishes", but its single assertion only checks the draft headline reads "Send it to", so the behaviour the block is named for is never tested.
findings.fix: In the copy success callback of states.publish (render-b.js, the navigator.clipboard.writeText(...).then branch around line 1815), before setting action.textContent = "Copied", add: if (F.publication.state !== "published") { F.publication = { state: "published", publishedAt: F.today }; F.updatedLabel = F.fmt.medium(F.today) + " " + F.fmt.year(F.today); var head = node.querySelector(".b-pressTitle"); if (head) head.textContent = F.project.name + " have had this since " + F.fmt.medium(F.publication.publishedAt) + "."; paintPublication(document.querySelector(".b-field")); } — and delete the now-duplicated, unreachable name === "copy" branch in wireOwner (render-b.js:1262-1288). Write the gate assertion first and watch it fail: from state=owner-draft click [data-act="publish"], then [data-act="copy"], then [data-act="owner"], and assert .b-shared reads "Live since 16 July · anyone with the link can read it" and [data-act="publish"] reads "Get the link"; on both grounds.

findings.problem: b.css:584 is [data-accent="structure"] .b-rail { background: var(--accent); opacity: 0.5 } with no exclusion for the backward measure, and it is declared 28 lines after the .b-back block, so it wins. Measured on state=day at 1440x960: the only rail on the wedding morning is 1x634px painted rgb(79,70,229) at opacity 0.5, identical on ?v=paper and ?v=ink. Everything hanging on that rail is behind the reader — Venue walk-through 14 days back through We said yes 274 days back — so on the one screen the whole company is judged by, the accent is spent drawing the past. b.css:552 states the opposite intent in its own words: "Quieter than what is ahead, and carrying no accent — nothing behind you is the next thing." The room's definition of this accent (lock.md, the founder's pick) is "indigo marks the next thing AND draws the part of the rail that is still ahead", and no part of this rail is still ahead. The morning then carries indigo twice with the two uses saying opposite things: .b-dayNow's 1px top border for what is happening now, and 634px of rail for what is over. This is a correction that enforces the lock, not a reopening of it.
findings.fix: Change b.css:584 to [data-accent="structure"] .b-measure:not(.b-back) .b-rail { background: var(--accent); opacity: 0.5; } and add, inside the .b-back block near b.css:556, .b-back .b-rail { background: var(--fore-16); opacity: 1; } so the past rail is drawn at the same hairline density as the ticks beside it. Leave the print override at b.css:1550 alone. Gate assertion first: for each of paper and ink, open state=day and assert getComputedStyle(document.querySelector(".b-back .b-rail")).backgroundColor does not contain "79, 70, 229", and that on state=phone the forward .b-rail still does.

findings.element: aria-label on .b-unfurl, states unfurl and publish, both grounds and both publication branches
findings.problem: The card paints "79" over "days away when this was sent", and render-b.js:1620 explains why in the file: "A chat client caches a preview at the moment it is sent, so the card has to be true a month later. The figure stays, because the distance IS the product, and the sentence under it says when it was true." The accessible name built beneath it reads "Mara & Finn, 79 days to Saturday 3 October 2026" — it drops that qualifier and states the cached figure as a present fact. So the one surface deliberately written to survive being stale announces itself, to the reader least able to check it against the visible card, in exactly the tense the visible copy was rewritten to avoid; and it is two grammars for one fact on one object, 40 pixels apart. Verified on state=unfurl and state=publish, on paper and on ink, and on the draft branch (owner-draft to Publish) where the label is identical. interaction-check.mjs:1636 asserts only that the figure appears somewhere in the label, so nothing here restates a gate.
findings.fix: In card() (render-b.js, the h("a.b-unfurl", { ... "aria-label": ... }) call), build the name from the same two strings the card paints: F.project.name + ", " + (said.state === "ahead" ? said.num + " " + said.unit + " away when this was sent. " : "") + (F.project.primaryDate.label ? F.project.primaryDate.label + ", " : "") + when. Gate assertion first, on unfurl and publish and both grounds: the label contains the .b-ogDate text verbatim.

findings.element: the kbd inside .b-undo, every owner state
findings.problem: The keycap beside Undo reads "Ctrl Z" on every platform. The document-level handler at render-b.js:1305 tests (event.ctrlKey || event.metaKey), and driving it confirms the product is not merely tolerant but correct on the Mac key: on state=owner-flight, open Send the invitations, press +7, then press Meta+z — the move reverses (.b-stepRead returns to "Saturday 8 August 2026 · in 23 days") and the bar empties. So the implementation already decided Macs exist and only the label failed to follow. A planner on a MacBook is told to press a key her keyboard does not carry, on the product's own advertisement of its way back; Linear, Stripe and Vercel all resolve this keycap per platform. The gate reads this node (interaction-check.mjs:432 and 2640) but asserts only its letterfit, never its text.
findings.fix: In undoBar() (render-b.js, h("kbd", { text: "Ctrl Z" })), derive the text once: var MAC = /Mac|iPhone|iPad/.test((navigator.userAgentData && navigator.userAgentData.platform) || navigator.platform || ""); and pass text: MAC ? "\u2318 Z" : "Ctrl Z". Nothing else changes — the handler already accepts both. Gate assertion first: with the context emulating a Mac platform the keycap reads "⌘ Z", and on the default platform it reads "Ctrl Z".

biggestWin: Judged as one document, the strings are the strongest thing in this lab. Every fact is said once, in one grammar, and the tense follows the clock rather than the fixture: the countdown answers with a state rather than a string, so "79 days" on a phone, "Today" on the morning and "The day has been and gone" afterwards are one object at one display step and cannot disagree; the ended page names the state without inventing a cause and dates the day forward or back depending on when it is read; the print sheet is the only surface that appends "on Thursday 16 July 2026" to its figure, because paper cannot be reloaded; the three refusals in the date field and the three in the first-run form are the same three true sentences rather than one scolding "invalid"; the ceiling stays enabled and says why; the retry sequence tells the truth at every step and refuses to print the same reassurance twice; the loading frame promises only what will actually render. The register is plain, declarative, sentence case, with no exclamation marks, no jargon and nothing salesy anywhere across fourteen states, six widths and both grounds — a full text harvest of ?v=paper diffed against ?v=ink is identical, so the copy is genuinely one document wearing two grounds rather than two rooms. On the forward surfaces the accent is also spent well: one hairline rule under the horizon, one filled tick on the next thing, and one pale rail for what is still ahead, which is exactly enough to make the instrument readable without reaching for a second colour.
